7. Section 46A was inserted in the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 by the Finance Act, 1995 providing for tax exemption to certain undertaking set up in Bangladesh between 1st July, 1995 and 30th day of June, 2000 (both days inclusive) provided it was, among other things, engaged in providing physical infrastructure facility and an application was made by it to the NBR in the prescribed form for such exemption within 180 days from the date of commencement of its commercial production or operation. It is noted from the record that the petitioner company was incorporated in 1986 under the Companies Act, 1913 to carry on, amongst others, the business of Container Depot Operators and of Container Freighting Station. The petitioner company applied for tax exemption before the NBR on 22-7-1999 under section 46A (2) (f) within 180 days from the date of its commercial operation. The said application of the petitioner company was rejected by NBR by order dated 18-10-1999, Annexure C to the writ petition, on a misconceived ground that the undertaking of the petitioner company was not providing physical infrastructure facility in disregard of its own field level enquiry report. Subsequently, the NBR recognised the undertaking of the petitioner company as Inland Container Depot (ICD) providing physical infrastructure facility as contemplated under section 46A by SRO dated 2-12-1999. 

 11. Delegated legislation may either mean exercise by a subordinate authority, such as a public department or a competent executive authority or the subsidiary laws themselves passed by such authority. The Act, of Parliament which delegates the power may, in so many words, provide that regulations, rules, orders or by laws may be made or approved under defined conditions. Such Act or statute may in some cases merely authorise such executive authority to appoint a day or fix some standard or to provide for some detail by way of example to carry out the purpose and intention of the legislation made in general terms. Delegated authority of the kind above referred to is required to be exercised strictly in accordance with the powers creating it and in the spirit of the enabling statute. The delegated authority is required to act strictly within the parameters of the authority delegated to it under the Act. The case of Ahmadabad Urban Development Authority vs Sharad Kumar Jayanti Kumar Paswala, AIR 1992 SC 2038 may be referred to in this connection. In the case of Me Eldowney vs Fords, (1969) 3 WLR 179, Lord Diplock observed: 

 12. When the rules are framed or any order is made, in exercise of delegated legislation, such rules, regulations and orders should be considered as embodied in the Act and forming part of it. Such rules, regulations or orders being subordinate legislation must give way to the provisions of the Act. In the case of Union of India vs Satyendra Nath, AIR 1955 Cal 581, it was observed: 

 "(13) I think we have now a complete picture of what the law should be. If the rules concerned were in the original schedule, then they were part of a legislative enactment in every sense of the word and, in such a case, the principle' might have to be applied, namely, that the later provision shall be effective. Here, however, the provision in the Rules has been effected by a non-legislative body under rule- making power. Therefore, the principle applied that by rule or regulation you cannot affect a provision of the Act, even though it is to be considered as embodied in the Act and forming part of it." 

 13. Rules, orders, etc. made by a subordinate authority cannot control the construction to be placed on the provisions of the Act. If reconciliation is found to be impossible between the section and the subordinate legislation, the latter is found to be in excess of the statutory power authorising the same the subordinate legislation shall be held to be ultra vires of the statute authorising such legislation, AIR 1943 Mad 617 and AIR 1968 Monipur 74. Where by a statute a power to make regulation is given to a public body, no regulation made under it can abridge a right conferred by the statute itself. The case of Municipal Corporation of Toronto vs Virg, 1986 AC 88 may be referred to on this point. A rule or a. by-law made under statute cannot, unless there are express indications in the statute itself, override or militate against the provision of the Act under which it has been framed; AIR 1967 All 173. 

 14. Where any subordinate legislation is made, normally it should be given prospective operation. But retrospective operation must be given if such operation is implicit in the language used in the enactment which conferred the power of subordinate legislation to a non-legislative body. In the case of Income-tax Officer Alleppey vs 1 MC Pon-noose and others, AIR 1970 SC 385, it was held that "where any rule or regulation is made by a person or authority to whom such powers have been delegated by the legislature it mayor may not be possible to make the same so as to give retrospective operation. It will depend on the language employed in the statutory provision which may in express terms or by necessary implication empower the authority concerned to make a rule or regulation with retrospective operation". In the Explanation to section 46A (2) (b) necessary implication is obvious that the legislature intended that clause I of the said SRO dated 2-12- 1999 should form part of the Explanation and it should take effect from the date section 46A was enacted in the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984.  15. There is yet another way of looking at the point involved in the present case. Where an exemption is conferred by a statute by an exemption clause, that clause has to be construed liberally and in favour of the assesse but must always be without any violence to the language used, 53 CWN 596 and AIR 1989 SC 501. If the tax payer is within the plain terms of the exemption it cannot be denied its benefit by calling in aid any supposed intention of the- exempting authority. The case of Hansraj vs Dave 1969 SCR 253 is an authority on the point. A provision intended for the benefit of the tax payer must be construed liberally in favour of the tax payer. The case of Nowab Gazzi vs Assistant Collector, AIR 1965 Audh 218 may be referred to on the point. Where any tax statute provides for any exemption of tax to some persons for a limited period, such statute must be construed strictly with regard to its charging provision, but once exemption or exception becomes applicable after resolving doubt or ambiguity regarding its applicability then full play should be given to it and it calls for a wider and liberal interpretation. 

 17. The principle of legitimate expectation, as argued by the learned Advocate for the petitioner company, does not appear to have any relevance or applicability in the present case inasmuch as the tax exemption available to the petitioner company is not because of any practice or principle followed by the NBR but because of the express provision of section 46A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. A case of legitimate expectation would arise when a body by representation or by past practice aroused expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfil. The facts of the case in hand do not admit of any scope of such argument. 

 19. This apart, the NBR sought to deny the tax exemption to the petitioner company by clause 2 of the impugned SRO dated 2-12-1999 by giving prospective operation. Such action on the part of the NBR is designed to deprive the petitioner company of the tax exemption under section 46A without any legal excuse and it is therefore, vitiated by malice in law; AIR 1966 Cal 151. Hence clause (2) of the said SRO dated 2-12-1999 is of no legal effect being void. It is observed in the case of Dr. Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh, 33 DLR (AD) 201 that if any act is committed on a legally extraneous or obviously misconceived ground it would be a case of "malice in" law". In this case NBR has refused to allow tax emption on an extraneous as well as misconceived ground by trying to recognise the undertaking of the petitioner company as providing physical infrastructure facility from 2-12-1999 instead of 1-2-1999 on the strength of clause 2 of the said SRO dated 2-12-1999 which is neither intended nor authorised by the statute, particularly section 46A thereof. Hence clause 2 of the said SRO dated 2-12-1999 is liable to be struck down.
